title: Optionals, enums and pattern matching
summary: An optional is a box that either holds a value or holds nothing (`nil`). It is just an enum with two cases, and `switch` lets you safely open any enum.
body: **In simple words:** In many languages any variable can secretly be null and crash you later. Swift makes "might be missing" part of the type: `String?` means "a String, or nothing". The compiler forces you to check before you use it.

**Real-life analogy:** A gift box. `String` is a gift you are holding. `String?` is a closed box: it may have a gift inside or be empty. You must open it (`if let`, `guard let`, `??`) before using the gift.

**How it works:** `Optional` is literally `enum Optional<Wrapped> { case none, some(Wrapped) }`. `nil` is `.none`. Optional chaining (`user?.address?.city`) stops at the first `nil` and returns `nil`.

**Ways to unwrap, safest first:** `if let` / `guard let` (check and use), `??` (give a default), optional chaining `?.`, `map`/`flatMap` on the optional, and last `!` (force unwrap: crashes if nil, use only when nil is a programmer bug).

**Enums are more than constants:** each case can carry data (associated values), enums can have methods and computed properties, and `switch` must handle every case. Adding a new case makes the compiler point at every place you forgot to handle. That is why enums are great for screen state: `.loading`, `.loaded([Post])`, `.failed(Error)`.
**Pattern matching:** `switch` can match ranges, tuples, associated values and conditions (`case .failed(let e) where e is URLError`). `if case` matches one pattern without a full switch.
keyPoints: Optional is an enum with `.none` and `.some(value)`; the type system forces you to handle "missing".
Prefer `guard let` for early exit, `if let` for a small scope, `??` for defaults; avoid `!` except for real programmer errors.
Enums with associated values model states that cannot be mixed, e.g. you cannot be `.loading` and `.failed` at the same time.
Exhaustive `switch` turns "I forgot a case" into a compile error. Avoid `default:` on your own enums for this reason.
`indirect enum` lets an enum contain itself (trees, linked lists).

code.caption: Screen state as an enum

mistakes: Force unwrapping (`!`) values that come from the network or user input.
Using several optionals/booleans (`isLoading`, `error`, `data`) instead of one enum, which allows impossible combinations.
Adding `default:` to a switch on your own enum, so new cases are silently ignored.
followups: **What is an implicitly unwrapped optional (`String!`)?** An optional that is force-unwrapped automatically on use. Used for IBOutlets that are set after init. Crashes if nil.
**Optional chaining vs force unwrap?** `?.` returns nil safely; `!` crashes when nil.
**How do you add a case to a public enum in a library without breaking clients?** Clients must use `@unknown default`; library enums are non-frozen.
**`map` vs `flatMap` on Optional?** `map` transforms the value if present; `flatMap` is used when the transform itself returns an optional, to avoid `T??`.
